Tribunal for adjudication: 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the action of the management of M/s. V K Enterprises, a contractor of IOCL, Indian Bottling Plant, 
Bangalore in terminating the services of S/Shri Ramesh S/o Late manjunath w.e.f. October, 2009, is legal and 
justified? What relief the workman is entitled to?” 


2 After registering the case as CR No. 27/202 notices were issues to both the parties. In response to notice 
the I Party and II Party No. | entered appearance through their respective counsel. II Party No. 2, even after having 
been afforded ample opportunities to mark appearance, kept aloof from the Proceedings and eventually is set exparte. 


3. The I Party filed Claim Statement stating that he has joined the service of II Party No. | and 2 on permanent 
basis on a month salary of Rs. [2.00 around 987 as General Employee and was put to discharge the duty of Loading 
and Unloading, Handling and other miscellaneous works. The action of the II Party was against the law and 
principles of natural justice. He is completely relying upon the earnings from his employment under the II Party. At 
the time of termination he was getting Rs. 6,000.00 as monthly salary. II Party has not granted any terminal benefits 
to him nor any notice of termination. He raised a dispute before the ALC(C), Bangalore against the II Party, but the 
latter did not take part in the conciliation, hence, this claim petition seeking an order directing the II Party to reinstate 
him into service and to grant terminal and other benefits to him as per law. 


4. II Party No. | contested the dispute maintaining that the I Party herein is not an employee of the II Party No. 
l corporation; he is a contract labourer working under the contractor II Party No. 2; the works of haulage and 
housekeeping were given on contract to II Party No. 2 V K Enterprises; the II Party No. 2 has deployed their 
workforce / labourers for carrying out the works undertaken on contract basis; it is the contractor who allots the 
works, supervises the works and pay wages, maintains Attendance and Wage Register of its labourers and complies 
with all statutory requirements covering the labourers under the ESI and Provident Fund Benefits . II Party No. | 
makes payment to the II Party No. 2 against the bills submitted by it; II Party No. | closed the operation of its 
Whitefield Plant w.e.f. 7.08.2009 and shifted the entire activities to Devanagonthi, LPG Bottling Plant and 
accordingly, the activities of Bangalore Plant / Whitefield were closed thereon. In the dispute raised before the 
ALC(C), Bangalore, I Party has clearly admitted to have been employed by II Party No. 2; he cannot make out any 


3050 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 8, 2026/CHAITRA 28, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


grievance about the termination or to seek any relief against II Party No. |. Hence, the claim petition is sought to be 
rejected. 


5. In addition to the query put in the schedule of reference, my learned predecessor in office has framed the 
following issues for trial based on the rival pleadings raised by the respective parties. 


“I. Whether the Indian Bottling Plant, Bangalore, in terminating the I Party workman is legal and justified ? 
2.To what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


6 Then the matter was posted for Evidence of I Party, the I Party filed an affidavit in lieu of his examination in 
chief on 26.05.20l7 and prayed for time to submit documents Thereafter despite having afforded ample 
opportunities, he did not prefer either to produce documents or to mount the witness box offering himself as a witness 
to prove the affidavit filed by him and to subject himself to cross-examination. Accordingly, the affidavit tendered by 
him is discarded from record by my learned predecessor as per the proceeding dated 22..209 and the case was 
posted for Evidence of the II Party. Initially Mr. Bishnu Minz, Chief Manager (Plant) is examined from the II Party 
No. | in chief. Since the said witness could not tender himself for cross-examination, the learned counsel for II Party 
took leave of this court to get the evidence tendered by him in chief examination to be struck off from record and to 
examine Mr. Girish Shimmoga Varadaraju, Chief Manager (Plant) as a witness on its side and got him examined as 
MW |. Despite repeated presence of MW | tendering himself for cross-examination, neither the I Party nor his 
counsel did turn up to cross-examine the witness. The individual notices issued to the I Party in person and to his 
counsel on board stood returned unserved with the postal endorsement “/nsufficient address” and “No such Person in 
this Address” respectively. As it is genuinely found that no purpose would be served by keeping the matter pending 
and by causing MW | to be present before this Tribunal anymore, this Tribunal is constrained to record cross- 
examination of MW | by the I Party as NIL and the case is posted for final argument. 


7. The Argument advanced by the II Party No. | is heard in detail. 


8. Issues No. | and 2: At the very threshold the learned counsel for II Party No. | urged by placing reliance on 
the verdict of the Hon’ble High Court of Allahabad in V K Raj industries vs. Labour Court and others (FJR Vol 59 
Allahabad 304) that as no evidence is produced by the I Party challenging the validity of his termination, he must fail 
in toto. In the ruling cited supra it is well settled that 


“if a party challenges the legality of an order the burden lies upon him to prove the illegality of the order, and 
if no evidence is produced the party invoking the jurisdiction of the court must fail. Therefore, whenever a 
workman raises a dispute challenging termination of his service, it is imperative for him to file a written 
statement before the Industrial Court setting out the grounds on which the Order is challenged and he must also 
produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or to produce 
evidence, the dispute refereed for adjudication cannot be answered in his favour and he would not be entitled to 
any relief and the court would be acting in excess of its jurisdiction if it gives an award in favour of the 
workman in such a case.” 


9. The entire back history of the proceedings of the case is revealed in the afore discussed paragraphs. The 
failure / refusal of the I Party to tender himself for cross-examination and also his failure to subject MW | 0 cross- 
examination has literally marked willful abandonment of the claim by the I Party or his absolute failure to put forth a 
valid and genuine case. The principle laid down in the ruling cited supra gives a complete answer to the query raised 
in the given case. Therefore, the only conclusion to be followed is that the I Party failed in proving a genuine cause or 
claim which leads to the total dismissal of the instant industrial dispute. 


0. With this view, these issues are answered against the claimant I Party. Hence, the following award. 
AWARD 


Reference is dismissed. Transmit.

is The Government of India, Ministry of Labour vide Order No. L-3002/29/202-IR(M) dated 06.08.20I2 in 


exercise of the power conferred by clause (9) of sub-section (l) and sub-section (2A) of Section 0 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, |947 (hereinafter referred as “The Act’) (4 of 947) referred the following Industrial Dispute to this 
Tribunal for adjudication: 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the action of the management of M/s. V K Enterprises, a contractor of IOCL, Indian Bottling 
Plant, Bangalore in terminating the services of Shri P. Varadaraju, S/o V Puttaraju w.e.f. June, 2009, is legal 
and justified? What relief the workman is entitled to?” 


3052 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 8, 2026/CHAITRA 28, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


2: After registering the case as CR No. 28/202 notices were issues to both the parties. In response to notice 
the I Party and II Party No. | entered appearance through their respective counsel. II Party No. 2, even after having 
been afforded ample opportunities to mark appearance, kept aloof from the Proceedings and eventually is set exparte. 


3. The I Party filed Claim Statement stating that he has joined the service of II Party No. | and 2 on permanent 
basis on a month salary of Rs. [4.00 around 990 as General Employee and was put to discharge the duty of Loading 
and Unloading, Handling and other miscellaneous works. On June 2008 when the I Party had come for work, the II 
Party refused to take him to service for no reason. The action of the II Party was against the law and principles of 
natural justice. He is completely relying upon the earnings from his employment under the II Party. At the time of 
termination he was getting Rs. 6,000.00 as monthly salary. II Party has not granted any terminal benefits to him nor 
any notice of termination. He raised a dispute before the ALC(C), Bangalore against the II Party, but the latter did not 
take part in the conciliation, hence, this claim petition seeking an order directing the II Party to reinstate him into 
service and to grant terminal and other benefits to him as per law. 


4. II Party No. | contested the dispute maintaining that the I Party herein is not an employee of the II Party No. 
l corporation; he is a contract labourer working under the contractor II Party No. 2; the works of haulage and 
housekeeping were given on contract to II Party No. 2 V K Enterprises; the II Party No. 2 has deployed their 
workforce / labourers for carrying out the works undertaken on contract basis; it is the contractor who allots the 
works, supervises the works and pay wages, maintains Attendance and Wage Register of its labourers and complies 
with all statutory requirements covering the labourers under the ESI and Provident Fund Benefits . II Party No. | 
makes payment to the II Party No. 2 against the bills submitted by it; II Party No. | closed the operation of its 
Whitefield Plant w.e.f. 7.08.2009 and shifted the entire activities to Devanagonthi, LPG Bottling Plant and 
accordingly, the activities of Bangalore Plant / Whitefield were closed thereon. In the dispute raised before the 
ALC(C), Bangalore, I Party has clearly admitted to have been employed by II Party No. 2; he cannot make out any 
grievance about the termination or to seek any relief against II Party No. l. Hence, the claim petition is sought to be 
rejected. 


5. In addition to the query put in the schedule of reference, my learned predecessor in office has framed the 
following issues for trial based on the rival pleadings raised by the respective parties. 


“I. Whether the Indian Bottling Plant, Bangalore, in terminating the I Party workman is legal and justified ? 
2.To what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


6. While so it is reported before this Tribunal that the I Party workman Mr. Varadaraju expired and the matter 
was posted for taking steps to implead his legal representatives. Despite having afforded ample opportunities no legal 
representatives of the I Party workman did come on record, the matter was then posted for Evidence of the II Party. 
Initially Mr. Bishnu Minz, Chief Manager (Plant) is examined from the II Party No. | in chief. Since the said witness 
could not tender himself for cross-examination, the learned counsel for II Party took leave of this court to get the 
evidence tendered by him in chief examination to be struck off from record and to examine Mr. Girish Shimmoga 
Varadaraju, Chief Manager (Plant) as a witness on its side and got him examined as MW |. As the I Party workman 
expired and no legal heirs have come on record to pursue the case, the Evidence tendered by MW | remains 
unchallenged. 


Pe Eventually the Argument advanced by the II Party No. | is heard in detail. 


8. Issues No. | and 2: The history of the case narrated above clearly indicates that the I Party could not pursue 
the case subsequent to the submission of his claim statement due to his untimely death. Though he was represented by 
his counsel until then, subsequent to his death the learned counsel did not take any effective steps to bring the legal 
heirs of the deceased workman on record. So literally this Tribunal is incapacitated to put on record any valid case of 
the I Party workman to be controverted by the contesting II Party. 


9. The factum of death of the I Party is seen recorded by my learned predecessor as per the proceedings dated 
5.03.207 as is informed by One Mr. Padmanabhan, who claimed to have worked with the workman Mr. Varadaraju 
that the latter expired about two years ago. Copy of the death certificate is not forthcoming from the side of the I 
Party. As already observed, no legal heirs have come on record to prosecute the case anymore. So much so, 
necessarily the claim stands abated as necessary steps have not been taken in time to implead the legal heirs / legal 
representative of the late workman or any steps to condone the delay in impleading the LRs and to set aside the 
abatement of the claim. In this scenario this reference is to be answered as the claim stands abated as the I Party 
workman died long ago without the matter being persued by any of the legal representatives. Hence, the following 
award. 


AWARD 


Reference is recorded as abated. Transmit.

2. After registering the case as CR No. 29/202 notices were issues to both the parties. In response to notice 
the I Party and II Party No. | entered appearance through their respective counsel. II Party No. 2, having been 
afforded ample opportunities to mark appearance, kept aloof from the Proceedings and eventually is set exparte. 


3. The I Party filed Claim Statement stating that he has joined the service of II Party No. | and 2 on permanent 
basis on a month salary of Rs. 450.00 on 02.02.989 as General Employee and was put to discharge the duty of 
Loading - Unloading, Handling and other miscellaneous work. On 06.0.2009 when the I Party had come for work 
the II Party refused to take him to service for no reason. The action of the II Party was against the law and principles 
of natural justice. He is completely relying upon the earnings from employment under the II Party. II Party has not 
granted any terminal benefits to him nor any notice of termination. He raised a dispute before the ALC(C), Bangalore 
against the II Party, but the latter did not take part in the conciliation, hence, this claim petition seeking an order 
directing the II Party to reinstate him into service and to grant terminal and other benefits to him as per law. 


4. II Party No. | contested the dispute maintaining that the I Party herein is not an employee of the II Party No. 
l corporation; he is a contract labourer working under the contractor II Party No. 2; the works of haulage and

ALC(C), Bangalore, I Party has clearly admitted to have been employed by II Party No. 2; he cannot make out any 
grievance about the termination or to seek any relief against II Party No. l. Hence, the claim petition is sought to be 
rejected. 


5. In addition to the query put in the schedule of reference, my learned predecessor in office has framed the 
following issues for trial based on rival pleadings raised by the respective parties: 


ढ॥. Whether the Indian Bottling Plant, Bangalore, in terminating the I Party workman is legal and justified ? 
2. To what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


6. Then the matter was posted for Evidence of I Party, the I Party filed an affidavit in lieu of his examination in 
chief on 02.05.20l7 and got himself examined as WW |. Despite having afforded ample opportunities, he did not 
tender himself for cross-examination. Accordingly, the evidence tendered by him in his examination in chief is 
discarded from record by my learned predecessor as per the proceeding dated 22..209 and the case was posted for 
Evidence of the II Party. Initially Mr. Bishnu Minz, Chief Manager (Plant) is examined from the II Party No. | in 
chief. Since the said witness could not tender himself for cross-examination, the learned counsel for the II Party took 
leave of this court to get the evidence tendered by him in chief examination to be struck off from record and to 
examine Mr. Girish Shimmoga Varadaraju, Chief Manager (Plant) as a witness on its side and got him examined as 
MW |. Despite repeated presence of MW | tendering himself for cross-examination, neither the I Party nor his 
counsel did turn up to cross-examine the witness. The individual notices issued to the I Party in person and to his 
counsel on board stood returned unserved with the postal endorsement “/nsufficient address” and “No such Person in 
this Address” respectively. As it is genuinely found that no purpose would be served by keeping the matter pending 
and by causing MW | to be present before this Tribunal anymore, this Tribunal is constrained to record cross- 
examination of MW | by the I Party as NIL and the case is posted for final argument. 


he: The Argument advanced by the II Party No. | is heard in detail. 


8. Issues No. | and 2: At the very threshold the learned Counsel for II Party No. | urged by placing reliance on 
the verdict of the Hon’ble High Court of Allahabad in V K Raj Industries vs. Labour Court and others (FJR Vol 59 
Allahabad 304) that as no evidence is produced by the I Party challenging the validity of his termination, he must fail 
in toto. In the ruling cited supra it is well settled that 


“if a party challenges the legality of an order the burden lies upon him to prove the illegality of the order, and 
if no evidence is produced the party invoking the jurisdiction of the court must fail. Therefore, whenever a 
workman raises a dispute challenging termination of his service, it is imperative for him to file a written 
statement before the Industrial Court setting out the grounds on which the Order is challenged and he must also 
produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or to produce 
evidence, the dispute referred for adjudication cannot be answered in his favour and he would not be entitled to 
any relief and the court would be acting in excess of its jurisdiction if it gives an award in favour of the 
workman in such a case.” 


9. The entire back history of the proceedings of the case is revealed in the afore discussed paragraphs. The 
failure / refusal of the I Party to tender himself for cross-examination and also his failure to subject MW | for cross- 
examination has literally demonstrated his willful abandonment of the claim by the I Party or his absolute failure to 
put forth a valid and genuine case. The principle laid down in the ruling cited supra gives a complete answer to the 


[भाग —ere 30) IRA HT राजपत्र : eT 8, 2026/चैत्र 288 ।048 i880 अप्रैल 8, 2026/चैत्र 28, |948 3055 


query raised in the given case. Therefore, the only conclusion to be followed is that the I Party failed in proving a 
genuine cause or claim which leads to the total dismissal of the instant industrial dispute. 


0. With this view, these issues are answered against the claimant I Party. Hence, the following award. 
AWARD 
Reference is dismissed. Transmit.

9. The entire back history of the proceedings of the case is revealed in the afore discussed paragraphs. The 
failure / refusal of the I Party to tender himself for cross-examination and also his failure to subject MW | for cross- 
examination has literally marked willful abandonment of the claim by the I Party or his absolute failure to put forth a 
valid and genuine case. The principle laid down in the ruling cited supra gives a complete answer to the query raised 
in the given case. Therefore, the only conclusion to be followed is that the I Party failed in proving a genuine cause or 
claim which leads to the total dismissal of the instant industrial dispute. 


0. With this view, these issues are answered against the claimant I Party. Hence, the following award. 
AWARD 
Reference is dismissed. Transmit.

2. Exparte 
l. The Government of India, Ministry of Labour vide Order No. L-3002/32/202-IR(M) dated 06.08.202 in 


exercise of the power conferred by clause (9) of sub-section (l) and sub-section (2A) of Section 0 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, |947 (hereinafter referred as “The Act’) (4 of 947) referred the following Industrial Dispute to this 
Tribunal for adjudication: 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the action of the management of M/s. V K Enterprises, a contractor of IOCL, Indian Bottling 
Plant, Bangalore in terminating the services of Shri K Prem Kumar S/o Late G K Nair w.e.f. June, 2009, is 
legal and justified? What relief the workman is entitled to?” 


2 After registering the case as CR No. 3/202 notices were issues to both the parties. In response to notice 
the I Party and II Party No. | entered appearance through their respective counsel. II Party No. 2, having been 
afforded ample opportunities to mark appearance, kept aloof from the Proceedings and eventually is set exparte. 


3. The I Party filed Claim Statement stating that he has joined the service of II Party No. | and 2 on permanent 
basis on a month salary of Rs. 45.00 around May 995 as General Employee and was put to discharge the duty of 
Loading - Unloading, Handling and other miscellaneous work. On July 2009 when the I Party had come for work the 
II Party refused to take him to service for no reason. The action of the II Party was against the law and principles of 
natural justice. He is completely relying upon the earnings from employment under the II Party. At the time of 
termination he was getting Rs. 6,000.00 as monthly salary. II Party has not granted any terminal benefits to him nor 
any notice of termination. He raised a dispute before the ALC(C), Bangalore against the II Party, but the latter did not 
take part in the conciliation, hence, this claim petition seeking an order directing the II Party to reinstate him into 
service and to grant terminal and other benefits to him as per law. 


4. II Party No. | contested the dispute maintaining that the I Party herein is not an employee of the II Party No. 
l corporation; he is a contract labourer working under the contractor II Party No. 2; the works of haulage and 
housekeeping were given on contract to II Party No. 2 V K Enterprises; the II Party No. 2 has deployed their 
workforce / labourers for carrying out the works undertaken on contract basis; it is the contractor who allots the 
works, supervises the works and pay wages, maintains Attendance and Wage Register of its labourers and complies 
with all statutory requirements covering the labourers under the ESI and Provident Fund Benefits . II Party No. | 
makes payment to the II Party No. 2 against the bills submitted by it; II Party No. | closed the operation of its 
Whitefield Plant w.e.f. 7.08.2009 and shifted the entire activities to Devanagonthi, LPG Bottling Plant and 
accordingly, the activities of Bangalore Plant / Whitefield were closed thereon. In the dispute raised before the 
ALC(C), Bangalore, I Party has clearly admitted to have been employed by II Party No. 2; he cannot make out any 
grievance about the termination or to seek any relief against II Party No. l. Hence, the claim petition is sought to be 
rejected. 


5: In addition to the query put in the schedule of reference, my learned predecessor in office has framed the 
following issues for trial based on rival pleadings raised by the respective parties: 


“I. Whether the Indian Bottling Plant, Bangalore, in terminating the I Party workman is legal and justified ? 
2. To what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


6. Though the case was repeatedly posted for I Party evidence, he did not tender himself as a witness at all, nor 
did he file any affidavit in lieu of his examination in chief. Accordingly, Evidence of the I party was held by this 
Tribunal as closed and the matter was posted for Evidence of the II Party. Initially Mr. Bishnu Minz, Chief Manager 


(ART ars 3(i)] __ भारतकाराजपत्र : अप्रैल 8, 2026/चैत्र 28, 948  .___ 3059 


(Plant) is examined from the II Party No. | in chief. Since the said witness could not tender himself for cross- 
examination, the learned counsel for II Party took leave of this court to get the evidence tendered by him in chief 
examination to be struck off from record and to examine Mr. Girish Shimmoga Varadaraju, Chief Manager (Plant) as 
a witness on its side and got him examined as MW |. Despite repeated presence of MW | tendering himself for 
cross-examination, neither the I Party nor his counsel did turn up to cross-examine the witness. The individual 
notices issued to the I Party in person and to his counsel on board stood returned unserved with the postal 
endorsement “/nsufficient address” and “No such Person in this Address” respectively. As it is genuinely found that 
no purpose would be served by keeping the matter pending and by causing MW | to be present before this Tribunal 
anymore, this Tribunal is constrained to record cross-examination of MW | by the I Party as NIL and the case is 
posted for final argument. 


7. The Argument advanced by the II Party No. | is heard in detail. 


8. Issues No. | and 2: At the very threshold the learned counsel for II Party No. | urged by placing reliance on 
the verdict of the Hon’ble High Court of Allahabad in V K Raj industries vs. Labour Court and others (FJR Vol 59 
Allahabad 304) that as no evidence is produced by the I Party challenging the validity of his termination, he must fail 
in toto. In the ruling cited supra it is well settled that 


“if a party challenges the legality of an order the burden lies upon him to prove the illegality of the order, and 
if no evidence is produced the party invoking the jurisdiction of the court must fail. Therefore, whenever a 
workman raises a dispute challenging termination of his service, it is imperative for him to file a written 
statement before the Industrial Court setting out the grounds on which the Order is challenged and he must also 
produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or to produce 
evidence, the dispute refereed for adjudication cannot be answered in his favour and he would not be entitled to 
any relief and the court would be acting in excess of its jurisdiction if it gives an award in favour of the 
workman in such a case.” 


9. The entire back history of the proceedings of the case is revealed in the afore discussed paragraphs. The 
failure / refusal of the I Party to tender himself for cross-examination and also his failure to subject MW | for cross- 
examination has literally marked willful abandonment of the claim by the I Party or his absolute failure to put forth a 
valid and genuine case. The principle laid down in the ruling cited supra gives a complete answer to the query raised 
in the given case. Therefore, the only conclusion to be followed is that the I Party failed in proving a genuine cause or 
claim which leads to the total dismissal of the instant industrial dispute. 


0. With this view, these issues are answered against the claimant I Party. Hence, the following award. 
AWARD 


Reference is dismissed. Transmit.

I Party : Kumara L, Advocate

2. Exparte 
is The Government of India, Ministry of Labour vide Order No. L-3002/34/202-IR(M) dated 7.08.202 in 


exercise of the power conferred by clause (9) of sub-section (l) and sub-section (2A) of Section 0 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, |947 (hereinafter referred as “The Act’) (4 of 947) referred the following Industrial Dispute to this 
Tribunal for adjudication: 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the action of the management of M/s. V K Enterprises, a contractor of IOCL, Indian Bottling 
Plant, Bangalore in terminating the services of S/Shri Ramasundaram, D.Rajendran, A.Ashok, S.Ramu, Smt. 
Pushpamma, smt. Lakshmamma, Smt. Premabai and Muniyamma during July, 2009 is legal and justified? 
What relief the workman is entitled to?” 


2 After registering the case as CR No. 26/202 notices were issues to both the parties. In response to notice 
the I Party and II Party No. | entered appearance through their respective counsel. II Party No. 2 stood served with 
notice, but kept aloof from the Proceedings even after having been afforded ample opportunities to mark their 
appearance. Eventually II Party No. 2 is set exparte. 


3. The I Party filed Claim Statement stating that they had joined the service of II Party No. | and 2 on 
permanent basis on a month salary of Rs. 6.00 as General Employee and was put to discharge the duty of Loading - 
Unloading, Handling and other miscellaneous work. On July 2009, when the I Parties had come for work, the II Party 
refused to take them to service for no reason. The action of the II Party was against the law and principles of natural 
justice. They are completely relying upon the earnings from employment under the II Party. At the time of 
termination they were getting Rs. 3,640.00 as monthly salary. II Party has not granted any terminal benefits to him 
nor any notice of termination. They raised a dispute before the ALC(C), Bangalore against the II Party, but the latter 
did not take part in the conciliation, hence, this claim petition seeking an order directing the II Party to reinstate them 
into service and to grant terminal and other benefits to him as per law. 


4. II Party No. | contested the dispute maintaining that the I Parties herein are not employees of the II Party No. 
l corporation; they are contract labourers working under the contractor II Party No. 2; the works of haulage and 


3070 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 8, 2026/CHAITRA 28, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


housekeeping were given on contract to II Party No. 2 V K Enterprises; the II Party No. 2 has deployed their 
workforce / labourers for carrying out the works undertaken on contract basis; it is the contractor who allots and 
supervises the works and pay wages, maintains Attendance and Wage Register of its labourers and complies with all 
statutory requirements covering the labourers under the ESI and Provident Fund Benefits . II Party No. | makes 
payment to the II Party No. 2 against the bills submitted by it; II Party No. | closed the operation of its Whitefield 
Plant w.e.f. 7.08.2009 and shifted the entire activities to Devanagonthi, LPG Bottling Plant and accordingly, the 
activities of Bangalore Plant / Whitefield were closed thereon. In the dispute raised before the ALC(C), Bangalore, I 
Parties has clearly admitted to have been employed by II Party No. 2; they cannot make out any grievance about the 
termination or to seek any relief against II Party No. |. Hence, the claim petition is sought to be rejected. 


Di In addition to the query put in the schedule of reference, my learned predecessor in office has framed the 
following issues for trial based on the rival pleadings raised by the respective parties: 


ढ॥ Whether the Indian Bottling Plant, Bangalore, in terminating the I Party workmen is legal and justified ? 
2. To what relief the workmen is entitled to?” 


6. Then the matter was posted for Evidence of I Party, Among the I Party workmen, Seven workmen have filed 
their respective affidavits in lieu of their examination in chief on 02.05.20l7 and prayed for time to submit 
documents. On 27.09.20l9 WW 3 was present and cross-examined by counsel for II Party. Thereafter, despite having 
afforded ample opportunities, WW |, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7 did not prefer either to produce documents or to mount the 
witness box offering themselves as a witness to prove the affidavit filed by them and to subject himself / herself for 
cross-examination. Accordingly, the affidavits tendered by them are discarded from record by my learned predecessor 
as per the proceeding dated 22..209 and the case was posted for Evidence of the II Party. 


7. Initially Mr. Bishnu Minz, Chief Manager (Plant) is examined from the II Party No. | in chief. Since the 
said witness could not tender himself for cross-examination, the Learned Counsel for II Party took leave of this court 
to get the evidence tendered by him in chief examination to be struck off from record and to examine Mr. Girish 
Shimmoga Varadaraju, Chief Manager (Plant) as a witness on its side and got him examined as MW |. Despite 
repeated presence of MW | tendering himself for cross-examination, neither the I Party nor his counsel did turn up to 
cross-examine the witness. The individual notices issued to the I Party in person and to his counsel on board stood 
returned unserved with the postal endorsement “Jnsufficient address” and “No such Person in this Address” 
respectively. As it is genuinely found that no purpose would be served by keeping the matter pending and by causing 
MW | to be present before this Tribunal anymore, this Tribunal is constrained to record cross-examination of MW | 
by the I Party as NIL and the case is posted for final argument. 


8. The Argument advanced by the II Party No. | is heard in detail. 


9. Issues No. | and 2: At the very threshold the learned counsel for II Party No. | urged by placing reliance on 
the verdict of the Hon’ble High Court of Allahabad in V K Raj industries vs. Labour Court and others (FJR Vol 59 
Allahabad 304) that as no evidence is produced by the I Party challenging the validity of his termination, he must fail 
in toto. In the ruling cited supra it is well settled that 


if a party challenges the legality of an order the burden lies upon him to prove the illegality of the order, 
and if no evidence is produced the party invoking the jurisdiction of the court must fail. Therefore, whenever 
a workman raises a dispute challenging termination of his service, it is imperative for him to file a written 
statement before the Industrial Court setting out the grounds on which the Order is challenged and he must 
also produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or to 
produce evidence, the dispute refereed for adjudication cannot be answered in his favour and he would not 
be entitled to any relief and the court would be acting in excess of its jurisdiction if it gives an award in 
favour of the workman in such a case.” 


0. The entire back history of the proceedings of the case is revealed in the afore discussed paragraphs. The 
failure / refusal of the I Party to tender himself / herself for cross-examination and also his failure to subject MW | for 
cross-examination has literally marked willful abandonment of the claim by the I Party or his absolute failure to put 
forth a valid and genuine case. The principle laid down in the ruling cited supra gives a complete answer to the query 
raised in the given case. Therefore, the only conclusion to be followed is that the I Party failed in proving a genuine 
cause or claim which leads to the total dismissal of the instant industrial dispute. 


Il. With this view, these issues are answered against the claimant I Parties. Hence, the following award. 
AWARD 
Reference is dismissed. Transmit.

“Whether the action of the management of State Bank of India, Tirupathi Zone in dismissing the services of 
Sri T. Manoharan, Ex-Messenger, is justified? If not, what relief the workman is entitled?” 


After receipt of the reference, it was numbered as ID No. 248/2002 and notices were issued to both the 
Workman and the management. 


2. The perusal of the claim statement filed by the Petitioner as well as the counter of the Respondent goes to 
reveal that this matter pertains to the termination of the Petitioner from service by the Respondent. The Appropriate 
government has not referred any industrial dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication in respect of termination of 
Petitioner. 


Section l0 (4) provides:- 


“I0(4):-Where in an order referring an industrial dispute to [a Labour Court, Tribunal or National 
Tribunal] under this section or in a subsequent order, the appropriate Government has specified the points 
of dispute for adjudication, [the Labour Court or the Tribunal or the National Tribunal, as the case may 
be,] shall confine its adjudication to those points and matters incidental thereto.” 


3074 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 8, 2026/CHAITRA 28, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Thus, in view of the above provision the Industrial Tribunal cannot decide a dispute not explicitly referred to 
it by the appropriate Government as it’s jurisdiction under Section l0 (4) of ID Act, 947 is confined to the specific 
point of dispute mentioned in the reference order and matter incidental there to. If the reference is for dismissal but 
the matter pertains to the termination, the Tribunal must strictly stick to the referred terms. 


3. Therefore, in view of the provision contained under Section 0(4) of the I.D.Act, 947, there is no reference 
of the industrial dispute regarding termination of the Petitioner for adjudication before this Tribunal. The reference of 
dispute herein pertain to the dismissal of the Petitioner from service. Therefore, this Tribunal cannot adjudicate the 
dispute in the absence of reference of termination by retrenchment of Petitioner.

I.D.Act, |947. Therefore, the claim of the Petitioner that he has been terminated illegally is not tenable and he is 
not entitled to any relief as claimed in the claim statement. Thus, Reference is answered accordingly. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

3062 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 8, 2026/CHAITRA 28, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Section 0 (4) provides:- 


“I0(4):-Where in an order referring an industrial dispute to [a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal] under 
this section or in a subsequent order, the appropriate Government has specified the points of dispute for adjudication, 
[the Labour Court or the Tribunal or the National Tribunal, as the case may be,]_ shall confine its adjudication to 
those points and matters incidental thereto.” 


Thus, in view of the above provision the Industrial Tribunal cannot decide a dispute not explicitly referred to it by the 
appropriate Government as it’s jurisdiction under Section l0 (4) of ID Act, 947 is confined to the specific point of 
dispute mentioned in the reference order and matter incidental there to. Ifthe reference is for dismissal but the matter 
pertains to the termination, the Tribunal must strictly stick to the referred terms. 


3. Therefore, in view of the provision contained under Section 0(4) of the I.D.Act, 947, there is no reference 
of the industrial dispute regarding termination of the Petitioner for adjudication before this Tribunal. The reference of 
dispute herein pertain to the dismissal of the Petitioner from service. Therefore, this Tribunal cannot adjudicate the 
dispute in the absence of reference of termination by retrenchment of Petitioner. Thus, Reference is answered 
accordingly. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

AWARD 


Matter placed today before Tribunal for order. perused the record. This industrial dispute was received 
from Government of India, Ministry of Labour by its order No. L-l202/442/200l-IR(B.I) dated 4.4.2002, which 
has been referred under section 0()(d) of the I.D. Act, 947 for adjudication with the following terms:- 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the action of the management of State Bank of India, Tirupathi Zone in dismissing the services of 
Sri M. Chiranjeevi, Ex-Messenger, is justified? If not, what relief the workman is entitled?” 


After receipt of the reference, it was numbered as ID No. 239/2002 and notices were issued to both the Workman and 
the management. 


2. The perusal of the claim statement filed by the Petitioner as well as the counter of the Respondent goes to 
reveal that this matter pertains to the termination of the Petitioner from service by the Respondent. The Appropriate 
government has not referred any industrial dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication in respect of termination of 
Petitioner. 


Section 0 (4) provides:- 


“I0(4):-Where in an order referring an industrial dispute to [a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal] under 
this section or in a subsequent order, the appropriate Government has specified the points of dispute for adjudication, 
[the Labour Court or the Tribunal or the National Tribunal, as the case may be,] shall confine its adjudication to 
those points and matters incidental thereto.” 


Thus, in view of the above provision the Industrial Tribunal cannot decide a dispute not explicitly referred to it by the 
appropriate Government as it’s jurisdiction under Section l0 (4) of ID Act, 947 is confined to the specific point of 
dispute mentioned in the reference order and matter incidental there to. Ifthe reference is for dismissal but the matter 
pertains to the termination, the Tribunal must strictly stick to the referred terms. 


3. Therefore, in view of the provision contained under Section 0(4) of the I.D.Act, 947, there is no reference 
of the industrial dispute regarding termination of the Petitioner for adjudication before this Tribunal. The reference of 
dispute herein pertain to the dismissal of the Petitioner from service. Therefore, this Tribunal cannot adjudicate the 
dispute in the absence of reference of termination by retrenchment of Petitioner. 


4. Even otherwise, Petitioner workman has failed to substantiate his claim of 240 days of continuous service 
in a calendar year just preceding from the date of his termination by any evidence in terms of mandate of Sec.25F of 
I.D.Act, |947. Therefore, the claim of the Petitioner that he has been terminated illegally is not tenable and he is 
not entitled to any relief as claimed in the claim statement. Thus, Reference is answered accordingly. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

AWARD 


The Government of India, Ministry of Labour by its order No. L-202/94/2000-IR(B.I) dated 9.07.2000 
referred the following dispute under section l0()(d) of the I.D. Act, 947 to Industrial Tribunal No.I, Hyderabad for 
adjudication and later the same has been transferred to this Tribunal bearing ID )२०.०१/2000, as per orders of Central 
Government vide Lr.No.H-!026/I/200l-IR(C.II) dated 8.0.200, requiring this forum to decide the question: 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the action of the management of State Bank of India, Anantapur Main Branch in terminating 
Sri K. Suryanarayana, Messanger, from the service of the Bank by way of oral Orders w.e.f. 3-03-]997 is 
justified? If not, what relief he is entitled?” 


After receipt of the reference, it was numbered as ID No. 94/2002 and notices were issued to both the Workman and 
the management. 


2. Before unfolding the factual matrix of the instant industrial dispute it would be apposite to have a bird eye 
view of a chequered history of the instant industrial dispute. Earlier instant industrial dispute along with the batch 
cases was decided by this Tribunal vide common award dated 7.5.2005 and the reference was answered in favour of 
the Respondent and against the Workman. That said common award dated 7.5.2005 was challenged by the 
aggrieved Workmen in various Writ petition No.6470/204 along with batch of writ petitions before the Hon’ble 
High Court of Andhra Pradesh and Hon’ble High Court vide its’ judgement dated 23.6.204 allowed all batch of writ 
petitions and set aside the common award dated 7.5.2005 passed in ID No.222 of 200I and other batch of ID cases 
by Central Government Industrial Tribunal cum Labour Court, Hyderabad and the Respondent management of State 
Bank of India was directed to reengage the Writ Petitioners in position, which they have been occupying prior to 
their termination and further directed to consider their cases for regularization as and when the substantive vacancy 
arises. This judgement dated 23.6.20l4 of Hon’ble High Court of AP, passed in WP No.6470/20l4 and batch 
petitions was challenged by Respondent management before the Hon’ble High Court in Writ Appeal No. 268 of 
204. The aforesaid Writ Appeals No.l268/204 and other Writ Appeals were decided by Division Bench of High 
Court of Andhra Pradesh by a common judgement dated 20.3.209. Hon’ble High Court in aforesaid Writ Appeal 
was pleased to pass the order which is extracted as below:- 


“ 7. Hearing the learned senior counsel for the SBI and the learned senior counsel for the contesting unofficial 
Respondents, we see that while the learned single Judge was justified in setting aside the award af the Tribunal, the 
proper course to be adopted was to remit all the cases to the Tribunal. This we say for reasons more than one. Firstly, 
in such matters, claims have to be decided on individual basis, as different persons have different claims as to the 
length of officiation or discharge of duties and functions; quality of engagement, drawings, accounting of the post for 
each one of them, who have worked etc. All these issues will not be the same in all the cases. Therefore, each case 
ought to have been directed to be decided by the Tribunal afresh on individual basis. The second and most important 
aspect is the learned single Judge has in one go ordered re-employment of all the workmen. This is not a relief that 
could have been granted without answering the individual issues; each issue relating to each case could not have 
been decided by the writ Court within the format of its adjudication procedures and scope. The adjudicating body, 
which has to do that activity, is the Industrial Tribunal. Therefore, we are of the view that while we would sustain the 
order of the learned singe Judge insofar as it interfered and sets aside the award of the Tribunal, the further findings 
and directions, issued through the impugned order have to go and the individual cases have to be sent back for 
consideration of the Tribunal. Such further procedure before the Tribunal will have to be carried forward with the 
materials already on record and also by affording an opportunity to the persons, who have claims as well as the 
management to place their rival contentions and further material before the Tribunal. The learned counsel appearing 
for the workmen are justified in pointing out that enormous delay has already happened and further action by the 
Tribunal in this line may be expedited. 


9. In the result, these writ appeals are ordered; 


(4) affirming the impugned common order of the learned single Judge to the extent it sets aside the common award 
dated /7.05. 2005 of the Industrial Tribuna!; 


(2) the further findings and directions issued through the impugned common order are vacated: 


(3) all the matters shall be remitted to the Industrial Tribunal with a direction to dispose of them within an outer limit 
of five (5) months from the date of receipt of a copy of this order; and, 


(4) the parties to make appearance before the Tribunal on the given date.”’ 


Thus, in view of the above direction of Hon’ble High Court of Andhra Pradesh in W.A.No.l268 of 204 and batch 
cases. This Tribunal has taken up the matter of industrial dispute for hearing and deciding it afresh in view of the 
aforesaid guidelines laid down by the Hon’ble High Court in Writ Appeal No.l268/20l4 vide judgement 
dated 20.3.09.

the Respondent Management terminating the services of the Workman by oral order dated 3.3.97 is unjust, illegal, 
violative of principles of natural justice and hence, the Management be directed to reinstate and absorb the Workman 
and to grant all incidental and consequential benefits.

Findings:- 

25. Point No.I:- Undisputedly settlements dated 7..987, 6.7.988, 27.0.988, 9..99l and 
30.7.996, minutes of conciliation proceedings and memorandum of understanding dated 27.2.!997 were executed 


between the State Bank of India and All India State Bank of India Staff Federation under section 2(p) and 8 (L) of 
ID. Act, 947 read with Rule 58 of Industrial Disputes (Central Rules), 957. 


Section 2(p) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 as follows:- 


(p) "settlement" means a settlement arrived at in the course of conciliation proceeding and includes a written 
agreement between the employer and workmen arrived at otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceeding 
where such agreement has been signed by the parties thereto in such manner as may be prescribed and a copy thereof 
has been sent to an officer authorised in this behalf by the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer; 


Section 8() provides as follows:- 
46, Persons on whom settlements and awards are binding. 


- (२) A settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and Workman otherwise than in the course of 
conciliation proceeding shall be binding on the parties to the agreement. 


Therefore, in view of the provision contained u/s.l8 (l) I.D. Act, 947, terms and conditions enumerated in the 
aforesaid settlements are binding on the parties to the agreement. The Learned Counsel for Workman has argued that 
the Workman after going through the selection procedure has successfully been listed in the panel for appointment on 
the permanent basis in the Respondent management and the empanelled list has to be valid till last person in the 
empanelled list is appointed on permanent basis. But the impugned order dated 25.3.97, 27.3.97 and 3.3.97, has been 
issued by Respondent management thereby the services of the Workman has been terminated and the said order is not 
in consonance of the terms of the agreement entered into between the parties. Further, Workman submits that the 
Respondent in the 5" settlement has mentioned the date i.e., 3.3.997 for lapse of empanel list which is illegal and 
that is not binding upon the Workman. The condition of lapse of empanelment list on 3.3.97 incorporated in the 
aforesaid 5" settlement, is arbitrary and illegal. 


26. The perusal of the impugned order dated 25.3.997 goes to reveal that the Chief/Branch Manager, SBI Zonal 
Office has issued the letter to all the branches with regard to the subject not to make any temporary appointments in 
the Branch in messengerial category from |.4.997. The extract of the said letter is given below:- 


“We have been advised by the Deputy General Manager, Zonal Office, Hyderabad that as both the panels of 
temporary employees of 989 and daily wagers/casual labours of 992 will lapse by 3.3.997, it has been decided 
by Central Office not to make any temporary appointments in messengerial category from |.4.!997.” 


Thus, from the contents of the aforesaid letter, it manifest that Head Office of State Bank of India vide letter dated 
25.3.997 has issued direction to all its branches not to make any temporary appointments in messengerial category 
from .4.997 due to reason of lapse of both panels i.e., 989 & 992 on 3.3.997 as per terms of settlements 
entered into by both parties. Further, the contents of the subsequent letter dated 27.3.997 issued by Respondent 
Management is also direction to Branch Manager, State Bank of India not to make any temporary messengerial 
category appointment with effect from |.4.!997 and it has also been communicated to all concerned that the panels 
of temporary employees and daily wagers maintained by Zonal offices stand lapsed from 3..997. Further, office 
order dated 3.3.997 has been issued by Respondent management that goes to reveal that the said office order has 
been issued to this effect that, “Consequent on absorption of temporary employees in permanent cadre, it has been 
decided by the competent authority that no one onwards, no further daily labour or temporary 
employees/appointments should be resorted to/engaged/employed.” Therefore, it reflects from the contents of the 
aforesaid orders that the temporary appointment in messengerial category and daily labour has been stopped by the 
Respondent management with effect from |.4.997 because of the lapsed of panel of temporary workers and daily 
wagers by 3.3.!997. The agreement for lapse of both the panels on 3.3.997 is contained in the 5" settlement 
which has been arrived at between the parties on dated 30.7.996 with the consensus of both the parties. Therefore, 
Workman can not challenge the terms and conditions contained in settlement dated 30.7.996 regarding lapse of 
panel on 3.3.997 as agreed between State Bank of India and State Bank of India Staff Federation. As per provision 
contained u/s.8() of I.D. Act, |947 the said Agreement dated 30.7.996 is binding on both the parties. 


In the case of Allied Sales Corporation Secunderabad vs.The Authority Under Andhra Pradesh..... 990 II LLJ 
50 AP para 44, Hon’ble Court have held:- 


“4. There was a settlement between the Management and the workmen under Section /650) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act on 25th April /963 under which the age of superannuation of the workmen was fixed at 55 years. The settlement 
was to be in force upto 30th June /966 and the next settlement, incorporating practically the same terms, was again 
entered into on 4th February 4967 under Section /6(/) of the Industrial Disputes Act. There is no dispute that these 
settlements are under Section /6(/), 


44, Now the Authority constituted under Section 4/(/) of the Act is an authority with very limited jurisdiction. It can 


3092 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 8, 2026/CHAITRA 28, 948 [Part II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


only decide in the first appeal whether a termination by the management is valid or not and is within the parameters 
of Section 40 of the Act. The said Authority, in our view, has absolutely no jurisdiction to decide whether a settlement 
entered into under Section /8(/) of the Industrial Disputes Act between the representatives of the Workmen and of the 
Management, is vitiated by undue influence or misrepresentation or coercion on the part of the Management. The 
Authority, namely, the Assistant Commissioner of Labour, was never intended by the A.P. Legislature to have 
jurisdiction to go into the question of the validity of a settlement arrived at under Section I8 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act by an Industrial Court. That Parliament has, in fact, constituted Industrial Courts under the Industrial Disputes 
Act, with extensive powers cannot be disputed. What we mean to say is that the Authority under Section 4767) of the 
A.P. Act has no jurisdiction what-so-ever either to question or to decide about the validity of any such settlements. If 
parties to a settlement have a grievance about the validity of a settlement, it is for them to agitate the matter before 
the appropriate forum and they cannot ask an Authority constituted under Section 4/(/) of the A.P. Shops and 
Establishments Act, /966 with limited jurisdiction, to go into any such question and, that too, incidentally while 
deciding whether retirement as per the contract of employment, is legal or not.” 


It is not the case of Workman that aforesaid settlements are vitiated by undue influence or misrepresentation or 
coercion on the part of the management. If the Workman feeling aggrieved by any terms of settlement/ agreement on 
the aforementioned grounds then he can challenge of settlement before a competent authority under the Act, 947. 
But here in the instant matter it is not a case of Workman that aforementioned settlement has been entered into 
between the parties on the ground of undue influence or misrepresentation or coercion. Therefore, Workman is barred 
to raise any objection in respect of fixing the date of lapse of both panels on 3.3.997 as agreed between both the 
parties and Workman can not challenge any terms of said Agreement. 


Further in the case of Herbertsons Limited Vs. Workmen of Herbertsons Limited and Ors, 977 AIR 322, 
Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


The Tribunal thought that the question of the quantum of membership of the 2nd Respondent did not call for a finding 
at all in view of Lhis Court's order. As observed above that was not a correct assumption. On the other hand, we feel 
that this view of the Tribunal has led it to approach the matter in an entirely erroneous manner. The Tribunal is, 
rightly enough, conscious that under section /6 (/) of the Industrial Disputes Act the settlement was binding on the 
company and the members of the 3rd Respondent union. Even so, the Tribunal devoted nearly half of its order in 
scanning the evidence given by the company and Respondent No. 3 to find out whether the terms of the settlement had 
been explained by the President of the union to the workmen or not and whether the workers voluntarily accepted the 
settlement knowing all the "consequences". This to our mind is again an entirely wrong approach. 


“When a recognised union negotiates with an employer the workers as individuals do not come into the picture. It is 
not necessary that each individual worker should know the implications of the settlement since a recognised union, 
which is expected to protect the legitimate interests of labour, enters into a settlement in the best interests of labour. 
This would be the normal rule. We cannot altogether rule out exceptional cases where there may be allegations of 
mala fides, fraud or even corruption or other induce- ments. Nothing of that kind has been suggested against the 
President of the 3rd Respondent in this case. That being the position, prima facie, this is a settlement in the course of 
collective bargaining and, therefore, is entitled to due weight and consideration. 


It is not possible to scan the settlement in bits and pieces and hold some parts good and acceptable and others bad. 
Unless it can be demonstrated that the objectionable portion is such that it completely outweighs all the other 
advantages gained the Court will be slow to hold a settle- ment as unfair and unjust. The settlement has to be 
accepted or rejected as a whole and we are unable to reject it as a whole as unfair or unjust. Even before this Court 
the 3rd Respondent representing admittedly the large majority of the workmen has stood by this settlement and that is 
a strong factor which it is difficult to ignore. As stated elsewhere in the judgment, we cannot also be oblivious of the 
fact that all workmen of the company have accepted the settlement. Besides, the period of settlement has since expired 
and we are informed that the employer and the 3rd Respondent are negotiating another settlement with further 
improvements. These factors, apart from what has been stated above, and the need for industrial peace and harmony 
when a union backed by a large majority of workmen has accepted a settlement in the course of collective bargaining 
have impelled us not to interfere with this settlement. That being the position, we unhold the settlement as fair and just 
and order that the award of the Tribunal shall be substituted by the settlement dated October 6, /973, The said 
settlement shall be the substituted award. The appeal is disposed of accordingly. There will be no order as to costs.” 


Therefore, in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above, the contention of the 
Workman that the date fixed for lapse of empanelled list on 3.3.997 for appointment to the permanent post vide 5" 
Settlement dated 30.7.996 is arbitrary, illegal is not untenable. The recognized union of Workmen has negotiated 
with the Respondent Bank Management representing large number of Workmen and the Workman as individual do 
not come into picture. Workman in the instant case has work as temporary Workmen in the Respondent Branch and 
in response of Notification he had applied for inclusion of his name in the panel and he was selected for inclusion 
his name in the panel list to be utilized for absorption of such Workman to permanent post in order of their seniority 
in the list. The Settlement dated 30.7.996 between State Bank of India and All India State Bank of India Staff 
Federation under Sec.2(p) and Sec.l8() of I.D. Act, 947 has clearly provided as regard non-messengerial position 
and it is agreed that all such posts sanctioned fallen vacant upto 3.3.997 shall be filled before empanel list is 


(ART are 3(i)] __ भारतकाराजपत्र : अप्रैल 8, 2026/चैत्र 28, ।848 i809 


allowed to lapse. Thus, in view of law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court, in the instant case, Agreement dated 
30.7.996 was entered into between both the parties in respect of lapsing of the both the panels on 3.3.997 and 
absorption of the Workmen from panel list was subject to availability of vacancy of post likely to arise upto 
3.3.997, have a binding force on Workman as well as management of State Bank of India in view of provision 
contained under section 8 () of I.D. Act, 947. 


Thus, Point No.I is answered against the Workman and in favour of the Respondent. 


27. Point No.II:- Firstly, it is submitted on behalf of the Workman that the Respondent has terminated his 
services by oral order on 3.3.997 without issuing any notice or paying any salary or compensation in lieu thereof. 
Therefore, the termination order of the Workman from service is in violation of provision contained Under Section 25 
F of I.D. Act, 947. Therefore, the order is liable to be set aside. 


28. On the other hand, Respondent counsel contended that Workman has not worked for 240 days in any 
preceding calendar year. Therefore, reference of the industrial dispute is not relevant. In this context, the Workman 
has examined himself as ४१४७] who has reiterated that Workman has been terminated from service by Respondent on 
3.3.997 without notice of salary or compensation in lieu thereof. Before examining the claim of the Workman on 
merit it would be apposite to reproduce the provision contained under section 25 F:- 


Section 25F provides:- 


Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen.- No Workman employed in any industry who has been in 
continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until— 


(a) the Workman has been given one month' s notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the period 
of notice has expired, or the Workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the notice: 


(b) the Workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days' 
average pay for every completed year of continuous service] or any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government or such authority as may be specified 
by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette]. 


Compensation to workmen in case of transfer of undertakings. 
Section 25B defines the term continuous service which provides 
Definition of continuous service.- For the purposes of this Chapter,-- 


(2) a Workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in uninterrupted service, 
including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or authorized leave or an accident or a strike 
which is not illegal, or a lock- out or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the Workman; 


(2) where a Workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (7) for a period of one year or six 
months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer-- 


(a) for a period of one year, if the Workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with 
reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the employer for not less than-- 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a Workman employed below ground in a mine; and 
(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


In order to prove the fact of 240 days of service within !2 months of a calendar year just preceding from the date of 
termination, the initial burden of proof lies upon the Workman and the Workman has to prove this factum by 
adducing his oral as well as documentary evidence in support of his claim. 


Further, how to calculate 240 days of service by the Workman in a calendar year. In this context the reference of 
decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court is relevant and the same are discussed below:- 


In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the Workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim was 
denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in the year 
preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor and that cannot be 
regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in fact the claimant had 
worked for 240 days in a year These aspects were highlighted in Range Forest Officer v. S.T. Hadimani (2002 (3) 
SCC 25. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record in that regard was produced. Mere 
non-production of the muster roll for a particular period was not sufficient for the Labour Court held that the 
Workman had worked for 240 days as claimed." 


3094 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 8, 2026/CHAITRA 28, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


In Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas (2004 (8) SCC 95), held "the burden was on the Workman to 
show that he was working for more than 240 days in the preceding one year prior to his alleged retrenchment." In 
MP. Electricity Board v. Hariram (2004 (8) SCC 246) the position was again reiterated in paragraph I as follows: 
"The above burden having not been discharged and the Labour Court having held so, in our opinion, the Industrial 
Court and the High Court erred in basing an order of reinstatement solely on an adverse inference drawn 
erroneously ..” 


In the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S Mani (2005) SCC Page 00, the 3 Judges Bench of the Apex 
Court held that "the initial burden of proof was on the Workman to show that he had completed 240 days of service." 


Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Mohan Lal vs Management BEL 98 SCC page 225 has laid down the 
principle that how to count 240 days of service within one year itis held: "Clause (2)(a) provides for a fiction 
to treat a Workman in continuous service for a period of one year despite the fact that he has not rendered 
uninterrupted service for a period of one year but he has rendered period of 240 days during the period of /2 
calendar service for months counting backwards and just preceding the relevant date being the date of retrenchment. 
In other words, in order to invoke the fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant 
date, ie the date of termination of service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained. move 
backward to a period of /2 months just preceding the date of retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the 
period of [2 months, the Workman has rendered service for a period of 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively 
answered in favor of the Workman pursuant to the deeming fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it will have to be assumed 
that the Workman is in continuous service for a period of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification 
enacted in Section 25-F" 


“॥4, We have already extracted section 25B since its amendment and the change in language is the legislative 
exposition of which note must be taken. In fact, we need not further dilate upon this aspect because in Surendra 
Kumar Verma_and Ors. v. Central Government Industrial-cum-Labour Court, New Delhi and Anr., Chinnappa 
Reddy. J., after noticing the amendment and referring to the decision in Sur _Enamel_and Stamping Works (P) 
Ltd case, held as under: 


"These changes brought about by Act 36 of /964 appear to be clearly designed to provide that a Workman who has 
actually worked under the employer for not less than 240 days during a period of twelve months shall be deemed to 
have been in continuous service for a period of one year whether or not he has in fact been in such continuous service 
for a period of one year. It is enough that he has worked for 240 days in a period of 2 months, it is not necessary that 
he should have been in the service of the employer for one whole year." 


In a concurring judgment Pathak J. agreed with this interpretation of section 25B(2). Therefore, both on principle 
and on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a Workman is not in employment 
for a period of 72 calendar months, but has rendered service for a period of 240 days within the period of /2 
calendar months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date, i.e. the date of retrenchment. If he has, 
he would be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of section 25B and 
Chapter VA.” 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above the initial burden of proof lies 
upon the Workman to show that he has completed 240 days of the service with the Respondent just preceding from 
the date of his termination. Further, in respect of the employment of calculating the 240 days service in view of the 
contents of Section 25-F read with Section 25-B of the I.D. Act, 947. 


29. Now, in view of the provision contained under Section 25 F and law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court, 
we have to examine whether the Workman has discharged his initial burden of proof in respect of his claim of 240 
days continuous service in a calendar year just preceding from the date of his termination i.e., 3.3.997. 


In this context, WWI in his cross examination has stated that, 


“I was not sponsored by any employment exchange. I did not undergo the regular process of selection before my 
appointment in the branch.” 


“I did not work for 240 days in any year in my entire service in the bank..”’ 


Thus, it is clear from the testimony of १४७] that the Workman had not worked for 240 days continuously in any 2 
months of a calendar year just preceding from the date of his termination in the Respondent bank. Therefore, 
Workman failed to establish his plea by his oral and documentary evidence that he had worked for 240 days 
continuously in calendar year just preceding from the date of his termination i.e., 3!.3.997. Thus, the claim of the 
Workman that he has been terminated by oral order without issuing notice or payment in lieu after termination, in 
contravention of Section 25 F of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 is not tenable. However the documents filed by the 
Workman in support of his claim, number of days worked with the Respondent goes to reveal that the Workman 
had worked intermittently as daily wager depending upon availability of work in branch. Workman did not file any 
document of appointment letter or salary slips in support of his claim for appointment as a non-messenger in the 


[भागत--खण्ड 303)| __ भारतकाराजपत्र : अप्रैल 8, 2026/चैत्र 28, 948 i809 
Respondent branch on temporary basis. 


30. Per contra, the Learned Counsel for Respondent has submitted the allegation of Workman that he was 
terminated from services is not correct. As the vacancies were filled up on regular basis in order of their respective 
seniority the non-engagement of the Workman does not amount to termination. Further, Respondent contended that 
no law provide that even though there is no work temporary employee should be continued in the bank work as the 
very engagement of Workman was subject to availability of work. Therefore, the allegation that the bank has 
indulged in unfair labour practice is incorrect. 


3l. Thus, in view of the fore gone discussion and contentions made by the Respondent, I find the force in the 
argument advanced by the Respondent that in the instant matter, Workman was not terminated from service by order 
dated 3.3.997 rather he was disengaged in view of the non-availability of the work in the branch. Further, there 
was direction issued by the Head Office of the Respondent authority not to engage any daily wager Workman/ 
temporary Worker w.e.f. .4.!997. Thus, such disengagement of Workman does not amount to termination. 
Moreover, the Workman failed to prove his claim that he was terminated in contravention of provision of Sec.25F of 
the ID. Act, 947 as he failed to establish his plea by any oral or documentary evidence that he had worked for 240 
days continuously in a twelve months of calendar year just preceding from date of termination i.e., 3.3.[997. 


32. Further, perusal of the order dated 25.3.]997 goes to reveal that the Chief Branch Manager, State Bank of 
India has issued the letter to Zonal Office with direction to all its branches to this effect that they have been advised 
by the DGM, Zonal Office, Hyderabad that as both the panel of temporary employees of l989 and daily 
wagers/casual labour of 992 will lapse on 3.3.997 it has been decided by central office not to make any temporary 
appointments in messengerial cadre from |.4.997, therefore it was directed to issue suitable instructions not to make 
temporary appointments from .4.997. There is no mention in this order that the Workman herein has been 
terminated from service by this order. 


33; Further, the circular dated 27.3.997 was issued by DGM, SBI to all branches in commercial network in 
respect of the non-appointment of temporary employees in subordinate cadre and it has directed not to make any 
temporary employment in the subordinate cadre with effect from .4.97 and further, it has directed to ensure that no 
temporary/casual/daily basis appointment of the petty cash. Further, it is directed to all Branch Managers that any 
deviation in this regard will be viewed seriously. Thus, these circulars do not reflect that the Workman has been 
terminated from service by this order. 


34, Similarly, office order dated 3.3.997 is simply a direction to all branches of the Respondent bank by 
DGM that no further daily labour should be engaged or employed. Therefore, the plea of the Workman that he has 
been terminated by the aforesaid order dated 25.3.997, 27.3.997 and 3.3.997 from the service by the Respondent 
is not acceptable. The evidence adduced by the Workman clearly goes to reveal that he had worked as a daily wager 
for which he has been paid wages according to number of working days. As there was an order for prohibition for 
engaging temporary workmen, in the bank, therefore, Workman could not be engaged by the Respondent for work 
from .4.997 and there after. It is settled law that the daily wagers are engaged by the employer depending upon 
the availability of work and as the work was not available the Workman was not engaged further by the Respondent 
management. Therefore, the Workman on the ground of number of days he had worked in the Respondent bank 
cannot claim any right to reinstate him into the employment. As the Workman failed to prove the mandatory 
condition of 240 days of continuous service as required under Sec.25F of I.D. Act, 947. Therefore, the 
disengagement of Workman from work can not be termed in contravention of provision contained under Sec.25F and 
25 B of the I.D. Act, 947. 


Thus, this point is answered against the Workman and in favour of Respondent. 


35. Point No.III:- In this context, the Workman has contended that the management failed to implement the 
selected panels during its valid tenure. The management adopted the back door methods contrary to the settlements 
and filled up the vacancies. The same is evident from the proceedings dated 8..993 a copy of the same is filed in

the issue by way of dispute, the management has refused to engage those candidates, the copies of call letters issued 
are filed herein along with claim petition. The Workman herein reiterates that the panels are meant for absorption but 
not for termination. In view of the same a duty is cast upon the Respondent management to engage the empanelled 
candidates like the Workman herein even in temporary vacancies till they are absorbed permanently in regular 
vacancies. 


36. On the other hand, Respondent has contended that the Federation approached Regional Labour 
Commissioner (Central) for implementation of bipartite settlement in respect of the absorption of temporary
